# PR Genius

> Somewhere in your GitHub there are PRs you have stopped opening.
>
> One needs a rebase you keep m

eaning to do. One has been red for four days and
> nobody told you. Three have sat untouched for thr

ee weeks. And one you avoid
> entirely, because opening it would mean confirming that it is dead.

**PR Genius is the board for that work** — the contributions you sent out into
other people's reposi

tories, where you have no tracker, no standup, and no
clue.

It is **not** a code reviewer. By default it never reads your diff, and it will
never tell you your

code is correct. There are good tools for that, and this is
not one of them.

**Unlike PR-Agent or CodeRabbit, this tool does not read your diff.** It does
not write review comme

nts on your code, and it is not an LLM. It scores a PR
against **61 anti-patterns** harvested from P

Rs that actually got rejected, and
answers a different question from the one a review bot answers.

It answers the question a working contributor actually has on a Tuesday
morning: **of everything I h

ave sent out, what do I touch today — and what
exactly do I do about it?**
## Why this exists
GitHub remembers the PR.

It does **not** remember why you closed your third attempt on a given repo.
What worked. What didn't

. Which reviewer actually answers and which commented
once and vanished. Whether the thing that got

you bounced last time was the
size, the missing issue link, or the tone.
That knowledge lives in your head. It dies when the session ends.
PR Genius is where it goes instead.

> A Repo Profile captures the **what** a project wants.
> A case study captures the **how** a contri

bution landed or died.
> Your own status history captures the **then-what** — how long it waited, wh

at
> changed, whether it ever came back.

Neither a code reviewer nor a chat model can have the third one. They see your
PR once, in someone e
lse's repo. This sees your portfolio over months.
## What it knows
| It knows | Why it matters to you |
| **How 67 large projects actually behave** — merge rates, review cadence, what gets closed | You st

op guessing what `encode/httpx` wants and start matching it |
| **Why real PRs got rejected** — writ
ten down, with the evidence | You stop repeating the mistake that already cost someone else three we

eks |
| **What your own PRs did over time** — which state each sat in, for how long | You find out a

PR died *while it was dying*, not three weeks later |
| **The policy of the repo you are aiming at*
* | A `Fixes #N` in the body is still the single most common reason a first PR gets bounced |

Numbers, for the sceptical: 753 loaded patterns, 190 harvested failed-PR
observations, 68 repo profi

les, 302 reviewed cases. Those are receipts for the
sentence above, not the point of it — every one

of them is verified against the
live tree on each release by `scripts/verify_claims.py`.

One of those corpora deserves a caveat: `success-patterns/` is
**retrieval/reference only** and is *

*not wired into scoring**. It is browsable
context, not a positive-feedback system, and no verdict h

as ever been changed
by it. The 61 anti-patterns are what actually move the risk tier.
## The nine states are nine decisions

A number on a dashboard tells you something is wrong. A *state* tells you what
to do about it.
| State | What it means for you today |

| `NEEDS_REBASE` | Twenty minutes of work and this PR is still alive. |
| `CI_FAILING` | It has been

red for days and nobody was going to tell you. |
[该节后续省略]
## What it will never do
Stated plainly, because the rest of this page is worthless if these are fuzzy:

- **It will not tell you your code is correct.** It does not judge your logic.
You can hand it a dif

f (`--diff`) and it will flag install commands, downloads
piped into a shell, and secret-shaped stri

ngs — a keyword pass, not a review.
Without one, it looks at the summary counts only.
- **It will no

t write or send anything on your behalf** unless you pass an
explicit `--confirm`. Every mutating co

mmand is dry-run by default.
- **It will not phone home.** Analysis is local: no LLM, no API key, no

network
call. The commands that touch GitHub do it with *your* token and only for PR
metadata. Ther

e is no telemetry — see docs/ADOPTION_DATA.md
for what is measured instead and why we chose not to b

uild the rest.
- **It will not pretend.** If a fact is not verified, the docs say so. This
page has

been wrong before and the corrections are in the
changelog.
## What this tool is NOT

The section above is about behaviour. This one is about **roles** — the jobs
people assume it does b

ecause of what it looks like. It does not do them, and
that is a boundary, not an oversight.
| It is not | What that means in practice |
| **A merge gate** | It never blocks a merge and never fails a job. The GitHub Action offers `commen
t_mode` and `apply_labels` only — there is no required-check integration, because a "gate" that can
be ignored is worse than no gate. If you want it to block, wire the Action's exit into *your* branch

protection yourself. |
| **A PR title linter** | It will not fail a PR for a malformed title. It wi
ll tell you that a missing `Fixes #N` is the most common reason a first PR gets bounced, and leave t

he decision to you. |
| **A CODEOWNERS-aware reviewer** | It does not know who owns which file, and

will not route or request reviewers. |
| **A code reviewer** | See above. It never reads your diff u

nless you hand one to `--diff`, and what it does then is a keyword pass. |
| **A positive-feedback s
ystem** | `success-patterns/` (692 of the 753 loaded patterns) is **retrieval/reference only** and i
s **not wired into scoring**. Only the 61 anti-patterns can move a verdict. |

The last row is the one worth internalising: the corpus is large, but the part
that *scores* is smal

l on purpose — it is the part backed by PRs that actually
got rejected.
